**Hard-to-vary report: Turing, "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem" (1936)**

**1. The question, frozen.** The paper answers several. Its title and opening put one central: which numbers can be produced by a strictly finite computing process, and where that class stops. The headline it argues (the "application") is: the class is exactly what a finite machine can print; it is enumerable; and no machine can decide, for an arbitrary machine, whether it keeps printing digits — so the Entscheidungsproblem has no solution. Frozen: *What can a finite computing process produce, and is there a general process that decides whether any given one produces forever?* Asked: a boundary — what cannot happen. Range: the computable sequences, over every conceivable finite process.

**2. The explanation, in parts** (in Turing's words). P1 the machine: tape of squares, one scanned square, finitely many states (m-configurations), move R or L, print or erase one symbol. P2 "circle-free" vs "circular". P3 "computable sequence": one printed by a circle-free machine. P4 the standard description and description number (S.D, D.N): a machine written as a number. P5 the universal machine U. P6 the erasable/scratch-square split (F- and E-squares). P7 the diagonal argument and its repair. P8 the machine Ji built from a hypothesised tester Θ. P9 §9's claim that the definition captures all "naturally computable" numbers. P10 the appendix: equivalence with Church's λ-calculus. P11 "not more than one symbol altered per move".

**3. Part by part.**

| Part | Mark | Because |
|---|---|---|
| P1 machine + states | Held | Remove the state and the machine prints only a fixed symbol; every §3 example needs it. *Built* — from analysing a human computer, §9.I. |
| P2 circle-free | Held | The whole contradiction turns on it; drop it and §8's target has no meaning. *Built.* |
| P3 computable sequence | Held | Sets the class under test; §8's result is that β is not in it. *Built.* |
| P4 S.D / D.N | Held | U needs a machine encoded as a number; the crux is K = D.N.(Ji), the machine fed its own number. Drop it and the self-application goes. *Built.* |
| P5 universal machine | Held | Ji must compute the sequence of the machine numbered N; only U lets it. No U, no engine for §8. *Built.* |
| P6 scratch-square split | Held (renamed) | The part that works is the *split* between permanent figure squares and erasable scratch squares; remove it and the universal machine runs out of rough-work room. But "alternate" spacing is **loose**: any convention reserving scratch space does the same job. |
| P7 diagonal + repair | Held | The pivot: without "β is not computable" the paper would be proving the false claim that the sequences are non-enumerable. *Built.* |
| P8 machine Ji | Held | The engine of the contradiction. *Built.* |
| P9 "captures all computable numbers" | Held if | The boundary result holds only if "computable" really means "machine-computable". §9.I is, in Turing's own words, "an appeal to intuition" — not testable. Settled by an independent account of what one finite step can be. *Asserted* (in part). |
| P10 Church equivalence | Borrowed | Rests on Church's "effective calculability", outlined in an appendix, not tested here. |
| P11 one symbol per move | Idle | Turing's own argument: any multi-symbol change splits into single changes. Drop the restriction and nothing is lost; it is stated for convenience, not as a limit. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**

*Change list.* In a proof, changes are changes to the conditions (by-domain §6): drop finiteness of symbols; drop finiteness of states; drop the one-symbol-per-move rule; drop the one-dimensional tape; drop the single scanned square; drop determinism (allow choice machines). Run one: drop finiteness of symbols → symbols differ by arbitrarily little, the machine cannot reliably read what it scans; the condition does work. What the list leaves out, and says so: whether "finite means" is the right reading of "computable" is not a change to the world — it is argued separately in §9.

*Flip.* The same machine model gives both the definition and the impossibility. Had the class turned out non-enumerable, the same parts would have served. So the model is not shaped to one outcome.

*Best rival.* The diagonal proof that the sequences are *not* enumerable is a real rival. Turing builds it and defeats it by locating the flaw (β is not computable) — a rival met with a real distinction, not a dismissal.

*Answer hidden in the starting points.* Unsolvability is relative to defining "general process" as "a machine". Turing states this plainly in §8. §9 exists to hold that definition in place; that is the soft joint.

*Where the jobs came from.* §9–10 add jobs: π, e, real parts of algebraic numbers and of Bessel zeros, and the numbers definable in the functional calculus. Each adds a class the model must reach and rules out a narrower rival. The model survives unchanged, so it reaches further — and is harder to vary for it.

*Pairs that pull.* Fidelity to a human computer (many symbols, many states of mind, two-dimensional paper) pulls against the finiteness that makes the proof work. Turing resolves it in §9.I ("not serious"). The line would be shown in the wrong place by a number plainly computable by finite means that no machine prints.

*Catch-alls.* The scratch squares carry "any" symbol — a bin in appearance, but the finiteness condition is its gauge: the machine prints from a fixed finite alphabet.

*Look inside.* §9 argues about the *workings* of a human computer (states of mind, observed squares, notes of instruction), not merely matching outputs — so the definition is not a bare table of results.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** One joint. Turn §9.I's appeal to intuition into a *built* argument, or replace it with an independent characterisation (Church's λ-calculus, or recursive functions). The appendix is borrowed; making that equivalence load-bearing rather than outlined is the single biggest tightening. Second: state the one-symbol-per-move rule once as a normalisation, so it is not mistaken for a load-bearing limit.

**6. What this does not show.** Passing is not truth. The negative result is relative to the definition of "computable"; the definition's rightness is argued, not proved. Nothing here settles whether a human mind is such a machine.

**7. One next step.** Try to exhibit a number computable by finite means that no machine of this kind prints, or an independent notion of "effective process" not equivalent to these machines. Either would move §9.I from assertion to test.
